## Introduction
On the 18 December 2002 the Swiss Federal Supreme Court (FSC) came to a conclusion, which disrupted the Swiss Electoral System. In BGE 129 | 185 the FSC criticized that in the elections for the Council of the City of Zurich, the thresholds for parties to win a seat varied heavily from district to district. Further did some districts have thresholds for parties to win a seat of up to 34%. Consequently, votes did not have equal effect, which undermines the electoral equality included in Art. 8 (Equality before the law) and Art. 34 (political rights) of the Federal Constitution. Based on this criticism the court decided that the City of Zurich had to implement corrective measures, but could choose their form. (BGE 129 I 185, E. 3, 7.3, 7.6, S. 199–200 ; Schweizerische Eidgenossenschaft, 1999, Arts. 8 and 34) The Government of the Canton of Zurich decided to keep the constituency structure (Regierungsrat des Kantons Zürich, 2014, pp. 3–4). Instead the canton of Zurich commissioned the german mathematician Friedrich Pukelsheim to develop a comprehensive and at the same time minimally invasive solution for the problem. Eventually Pukelsheim came up with a method called "biproportional divisor method with standard rounding" which is today often simply called "Double Pukelsheimer" or "Biproportional apportionment". (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 9-10)

The distinguishing feature of the Pukelsheimer Proporz, is that it through the so called upper-apportionment artificially creates a single electoral district for the initial allocation of the parliamentary seats to the parties or list groups. Through this mechanism, the difference between seat and voteshares gets minimized and with that also the effective threshold for parties to enter the parliament gets lowered. (Lüscher, 2023, p. 575)

Through its upper-apportionment mechanism and the lowered threshold, the reform is especially relevant for the representation of smaller parties, since votes that would previously have been ineffective in small constituencies can now contribute to a seat gain at the cantonal level. Sandro Lüscher illustrates this mechanical effect with the case of Schwyz in 2016: under the old Hagenbach-Bischoff system, the Green Liberal Party would not have won a single seat, whereas under the new method they obtained three seats (Lüscher, 2025, p. 1-3).

Since Zurich first used the system in 2007, eight further cantons have used it: Schaffhausen (2008), Aargau (2009), Nidwalden (2014), Zug (2014), Schwyz (2016) , Valais (2017) , Uri (2020), Graubünden (2022). In 2025 also the voters from Basel Landschaft decided to implement the Biproportional apportionment from 2027 on (Lüscher , 2024, p.17 ; Kanton Basel-Landschaft, 2025a, p.7 ; Kanton Basel-Landschaft, 2025b) While nine of these cantons already implemented the algorithm, more cantons are currently discussing the implementation too. In Thurgau, the initiative "Mehr Transparenz bei Wahlen im Thurgau" is currently pending at the Grand Council of the Canton and a special parliamentary committee is currently examining the iniatitive, also in the canton of Lucerne, the iniatitive "Faire Wahlen ohne Listenflut" was submitted and the voters will be able to decide on the effectuation (Grosser Rat des Kantons Thurgau, n.d.; Regierungsrat des Kantons Luzern, 2026, pp. 19–20). In the canton of St.Gallen in 2026 an initiative to adapt the algorithm was launched (Initiativkomitee «Damit jede Stimme zählt», n.d.).

The amount of cantons who have already implemented the system or are debating about doing so, suggets that the decision by the FSC had a substantial impact on how Swiss citizens elect their regional parliaments. It seems that the double-Pukelsheimer through its wide implementation across cantons is a success story. Since the first election under double Pukelsheim in Zurich in 2007, the system has been used in 32 cantonal parliamentary elections.^[The 32 elections comprise Zurich (2007, 2011, 2015, 2019, and 2023; Amt für Statistik und Daten Kanton Zürich, 2026); Schaffhausen (2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024; Kanton Schaffhausen, n.d.; Staatskanzlei Kanton Schaffhausen, 2020, 2024); Aargau (2009, 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024; Department für Finanzen und Ressourcen des Kantons Aargau, 2009; Regierungsrat des Kantons Aargau, 2013; Statistisches Amt Kanton Aargau, n.d.); Nidwalden (2014, 2018, 2022, and 2026; Staatskanzlei Nidwalden, 2014, 2018, 2022, 2026); Zug (2014, 2018, and 2022; Kanton Zug, 2022a, 2022b, 2022c); Schwyz (2016, 2020, and 2024; Bundesgericht, 2012); Valais (2017, 2021, and 2025; Kanton Wallis, 2016, 2020, 2024; Staat Wallis, 2017); Uri (2020 and 2024; Standeskanzlei Uri, 2024a, 2024b); and Graubünden (2022 and 2026; Kanton Graubünden, 2022, 2026).]

Taken together, this number of elections and almost 20 years of experience provide a reason to evaluate the impact of the reform, especially on smaller parties. How much has the reform changed smaller parties seat shares and how large is the actual difference in seat allocation between the Hagenbach-Bischoff and Double Pukelsheim system? Are there other major differences, for example in how the reform performs in smaller versus larger parliaments, and how does the smaller parties seat share and gain evolve across successive elections?

Existing research primarily examines Double Pukelsheim in legal, normative, or system-level terms. A few studies also conduct counterfactual comparisons, but these cover either individual elections or only one election per canton (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, pp. 1590–1592; Leuzinger, 2018, p. 42; Lüscher, 2024, p. 13). Although their results indicate that smaller parties can benefit from Double Pukelsheim, the magnitude and consistency of this mechanical allocation difference across successive elections remain less systematically examined.

This thesis addresses this gap by applying a consistent Hagenbach–Bischoff counterfactual to 30 elections in eight transition cantons. Two Graubünden elections are presented as contextual comparisons but excluded from the main transition estimate. Holding the observed post-reform votes and list structure constant, the analysis measures the difference in the share of seats won by smaller electoral lists and examines variation across institutional settings and successive elections.

## Theory and Literature Review

### Institutional and Theoretical Background

This chapter provides the institutional and theoretical background for analyzing the transition from Hagenbach-Bischoff to Double Pukelsheim and reviews the relevant literature. It first outlines the historical development of electoral systems in Switzerland and then explains the functioning and limitations of the Hagenbach-Bischoff and Double Pukelsheim methods. It subsequently examines the adoption and canton-specific implementation of Double Pukelsheim. Finally, the literature review situates this thesis within previous research before the expected effects of the transition are derived.

#### Historical Development

Until the late nineteenth century swiss voters elected the regional parliaments and great councils only under majority voting. In a majority voting system, the candidates or parties who receive the relative or absolute majority receive the seats, therefore this systematically favours the dominant parties. The disadvantages for smaller parties let some of the political minorities demand, to change to a proportional electoral system. In 1891 the canton of Ticino, was the first one to use a PR-System to vote for their Grand Council, till the end of World War I , 7 1/2 more cantons had followed. When the socialist and conservative minorities on their third attempt in 1918 achieved, that the National Council will be elected through a proportional system, it boosted the general adoption of it across Switzerland. Most of the cantons Grand Councils aswell as the National Council were then elected with the Hagenbach-Bischoff proportional system. In the beginning of the 21th century, the cantons of Graubünden and Appenzell Innerrhoden were the only ones to still vote their parliaments with the majority system.  (Gilg, 2014, “Mehrheits- und Verhältniswahl” section ; Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 2) Nowadays the Kanton Appenzell Innerrhoden is the only remaining canton still voting the Grand Council by majority voting (Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p. 18). It can therefore be said, that proportional systems are the dominating electoral systems for cantonal parliaments in Switzerland. 

In the last 20 years the prior dominance of the Hagenbach-Bischoff system has been demolished by the wide implementation of the DP. As of 2025, eleven cantons distribute the parliamentary seats with Hagenbach-Bischoff and ten cantons implemented the DP, two cantons namely Glarus and Basel-Landschaft use the Sainte-Laguë method and two namely Ticino and Vaud use the Hare/Niemeyer method (Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p.18). Of the nine cantons analyzed here, eight previously used Hagenbach-Bischoof for at least the majority of their parliamentary seats, only Graubünden priorly used majority voting throughout. Zug's Neuheim constituency and Uri's smaller municipalities also used Majorz rather than Hagenbach-Bischoff (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, Table 1; Bundesgericht, 2010b, E. 5.1; Standeskanzlei Uri, 2020, p. 1; Statistisches Amt des Kantons Zürich, 2011, p. 286; Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 2007, p. 6; Regierungsrat des Kantons Aargau, 2007, p. 18). 

#### The Hagenbach-Bischoff Method 

To be able to understand later the differences between the HB and the DP Method one has to understand the allocation under the priorly used Hagenbach-Bischoff system. 

Under Hagenbach-Bischoff, seats are allocated separately in each constituency. Let $M$ denote the number of seats in the constituency, $v_i$ the votes for an eligible list $i$, and $V$ the total list votes used to calculate the distribution number. The distribution number $D$ is the smallest integer strictly greater than $V/(M+1)$. In the first allocation, each list receives the integer part of its votes divided by $D$ (Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p. 41):

```{=typst}
$ D = floor(V / (M + 1)) + 1, quad s_i = floor(v_i / D). $
```

If the first allocation leaves seats unassigned, the remaining seats are awarded one at a time. For each list, its votes are divided by the number of seats it currently holds plus one. The list with the highest quotient receives the next seat; its quotient $h_i$ and the allocated seats $s_i$ are then recalculated, and the process continues until all $M$ seats have been filled:

```{=typst}
$ h_i = v_i / (s_i + 1). $
```
 This calculation yields the same allocation as the D'Hondt divisor method with downward rounding (Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p. 41). List alliances, eligibility thresholds, and rules for resolving equal quotients depend on the applicable electoral law. The counterfactual in this thesis applies the relevant former cantonal rules within each constituency, as detailed in the [Data Cleaning section](#data-cleaning).

 The central weakness of the traditional cantonal application of Hagenbach–Bischoff does not arise solely from the allocation formula, but from applying it separately in constituencies that often have few seats. Small district magnitudes create high and geographically varying natural thresholds, meaning that votes for smaller parties may fail to contribute to a seat and cannot be pooled across the canton. This can impair equality of electoral success and systematically disadvantage smaller parties. As shown in the later section on the adoption of Double Pukelsheim, these inequalities were central to the legal and political debates that led several cantons to adopt Double Pukelsheim. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, pp. 507-508, 521; Bundesgericht, 2002, E. 7.1.1 and 7.6.2)

#### The Double Pukelsheimer Method

Based on the weaknesses of the Hagenbach-Bischoff Method and the FSC decision, the canton of Zurich comissioned the mathematician Friedrich Pukelsheim to develop a new method (Lüscher, 2024, p.10). The following section explores how the algorithm works and how it makes sure that it complies with the Federal Law and mitigates the HB weaknesses.

Based on Article 8 and 34 of the Federal Constitution, there are three principles which have to be followed. These are principle of equal voting value, equality of voting power and equality of electoral value. The equal voting value ensures that each voter within an electoral district gets allocated the identical number of votes. The second principle is the equality of voting power (voting weight guarantee). This requires the population represented per seat to be approximately equal across electoral districts.  Thirdly there is the equality of electoral success, which should assure, that all votes contribute equally to the election and that as many votes as possible are taken into account in the allocation of seats. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, pp. 506-507) The equality of electoral success is violated, when the natural quorum (threshold) in a district is too high, this is given when there are less than 9 mandates within a district. Since then the threshold is higher than the 10% maximum given the FSC jurisdiction and it's calculation method, 1/(M+1) with "M" being the number of mandates. (Pukelsheim & Schuchmacher, 2004, p. 505 ; Bundesgericht, 2005, Regeste) Equality of counting value concerns the formal treatment of votes, while equality of voting power depends on the separately determined ratio of population to seats in each electoral district (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, pp. 507, 515–516). For the traditional application of Hagenbach–Bischoff, the main difficulty lies in equality of electoral success when small districts impose high natural thresholds (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 508; Bundesgericht,2002, E. 7.1.1 and 7.6.2). 

To approach this main issue of the Hagenbach-Bischoff, the Double Pukelsheimer or originally called the "Neues Zürcher Zuteilungsverfahren" knows a upper and a lower apportionment (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p.513). 

- **Upper Apportionment** To bypass the natural quorums, in the upper apportionment, the whole canton is seen as one single district. All the seats are then allocated towards the parties. For that the votes from the district-level have to be summarized on a cantonal level, there the first difficulty emerges. Since the district magnitudes vary, the voters also have a different amount of votes, depending on from which canton they are from. Therefore to be able to summarize on a global level, the following is done. The number of party votes per constituency are taken and divided with the respective number of seats. The resulting quotient gets rounded to the next number and indicates the amount of voters per list. The rounded quotients, can then be summed across all districts and divided by the cantonal divisor to get each parties total seats. The divisor is set by an official authority, in Zurich e.g. its the Department of the Government Councillor which is responsible for the elections. The department needs to assure, that with the set divisor exactly as many seats can be allocated as there are available. The number of seats which result per party, are rounded again to the next number. (Pukelsheim & Schuchmacher, 2011, p.1584-1585 ; Kanton Zürich, 2003, § 10 and 103)

- **Lower Apportionment** This step assigns each party's cantonwide seats from the upper apportionment to its district lists while preserving each district's predetermined seat total. First, the party votes in each district are divided by a district divisor chosen so that the rounded results add up to the district's seats. These initial allocations may not match the parties' cantonwide entitlements: in the 2011 Zurich election, the SVP would have received 55 seats instead of the 54 assigned in the upper apportionment. To correct such differences, every district list of a party is divided by the same additional list group divisor. A divisor above one reduces the party's unrounded quotients and can remove seats while a divisor below one can add seats. Consider a hypothetical SVP list in District Y whose quotient after division by the district divisor is 2.51, giving it three seats after rounding. If increasing the SVP's list group divisor to 1.01 changes no other SVP list's rounded allocation, this quotient falls to $2.51/1.01 \approx 2.49$, so the list receives two seats and the SVP's total seats match the ones from the upper apportionment. This change though may leave District Y one seat short, requiring an adjustment to its district divisor. The party and district divisors are then adjusted in turn until every party receives its cantonwide entitlement and every district retains its fixed number of seats. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, pp. 1585–1586)

To summarize, the upper apportionment in the Double Pukelsheim system reduces inequalities in electoral success caused by the high natural thresholds of small constituencies under the previous district-by-district Hagenbach-Bischoff system. It does so by pooling parties votes across the canton before seats are assigned to constituencies. This is also the main improvement of DP regarding the three principles in contrast to Hagenbach-Bischoff. 

##### Trade-offs and Criticisms

Alike every proportional system, also the Double Pukelsheimer system has its flaws for which it gets criticized. One of the main weaknesses of the biproprtional apportionment compared to the HB System is its complexity. It gets mentioned throughout, that its relatively difficult to understand the system holistically and that there is  profound knowledge needed, to be able to compute the seat allocation. (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 19 ; Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p.24 ; Lüscher, 2024, p.20) Lüscher tough mentions, that the usage of list alliances under the Hagenbach-Bischoff method also led to a high complexity situation. This especially since, beforehand the election it was impossible to estimate, which party would profit from the alliance. (Lüscher, 2024, p.20) Another main point of criticism, are the so called "discordant seat allocations". The discordant seat allocations describe the phenomena when within a district a party wins more seats than another party with more votes in that district. This phenomena can appear through the lower apportionment process and the dual role of the system to achieve both proportionality canton wide and within a district. The emerging situation, can cause confusement and frustration especially within the party which initially received more votes in that specific constituency. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 519) Not only for the parties themself it can be irritating, but also for the voters. This especially since in Switzerland elections often contain a personal vote component, if then a popular figure from one party, loses its seat to a less known figure from another party and district, this may raise concerns. A reaction to this flaw of the DP-System, was that the cantons of Zug, Schaffhausen and Graubünden implemented a majority clause, which ensures that the most popular party in the corresponding constituency receives atleast one seat. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 21) Pukelsheimer, himself was already aware of this issue in 2004 and pointed out that the so called majority requirement can in rare ocassions be not fulfilled. On base of this he mentioned the possibility of the implementation of such a majority clause. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 520) Another issue of the system, is that different turnout level and different proportions of residents who are eligible to vote in the consituencies can determine the allocated mandates of other constituencies. To illustrate this , Lüscher provides an example: There are three Districts with the same size and number of mandates, but while District 1 produces 50% of all votes, District 2 and 3 only produce each 25%. Through this District 1 determines 50% of the canton-wide party result, while only having 33.3% of the mandates. Subsequently this leads to under- and overrepresentation in the corresponding districts. (Lüscher, 2023, pp. 578-579) One other point was often discussed to be a possible weaknes of the Double Pukelsheim: Party System Fragmentation. For example both reports of the Swiss Federal Chancellery in 2013 and 2025 mention the possible party fragmentation in parliaments. As a possible measure to prevent fragmentation, the implentation of thresholds is mentioned.  (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p.18 ; Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p. 24) Though Lüscher, came in his Thesis to the perception, that the general trend of a rising amount of parties in swiss cantonal parliaments, is unrelated to the implementation of the Double Pukelsheim. He then also mentioned, that the inexistency of an effect, might come from that several cantons have implemented thresholds. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 135) Therefore it can't be conclusively stated, whether the reform would have had an impact on party system fragmentation without the implentation of thresholds or not. 

Taken together, these criticisms illustrate the central trade-off of Double Pukelsheim. Although the system improves canton-wide proportionality and reduces the number of ineffective votes, it does so at the cost of greater computational complexity and potentially counterintuitive outcomes at the constituency level. Majority clauses and electoral thresholds can mitigate discordant seat allocations and party-system fragmentation, but may simultaneously weaken proportionality. The system therefore does not eliminate electoral distortions entirely, it rather prioritizes party proportionality and equal vote success over simplicity and fully autonomous constituency-level representation.

#### The Adoption of Double Pukelsheim in Swiss Cantons
In the following paragraphs the arguments brought up in each reform canton will be discussed in chronological order. The year in the beginning of each entry, marks the year of first application of the double Pukelsheimer in the corresponding canton. 

- **2007:** Zurich became the first canton to use Double Pukelsheim, which it had commissioned Friedrich Pukelsheim to develop. The reform followed a 2002 voting-rights complaint about elections to Zurich's city parliament. The Swiss Federal Supreme Court partially upheld the complaint. It found that the thresholds in some districts with up to 33% were massively above the 10% threshold, which is seen as compatible with the prinicples of proportional representation. Further was it claimed, that thresholds vary to much between districts. The ruling mandated the canton of Zurich to reform the system, subsequently it then implemented the Pukelsheimer Proporz with a 5% district level threshold for parties to enter the parliament. (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 9–10, 33-36) In 2021, Zurich added a 3% cantonwide threshold, first applied in the 2023 election. A change to how that threshold is calculated was adopted in 2025 and will first apply in the 2027 election (Regierungsrat des Kantons Zürich, 2024, pp. 2, 5; Regierungsrat des Kantons Zürich, 2025, p. 1).

- **2008:** Schaffhausen: In a 2004 popular vote, Schaffhausen’s electorate approved a reduction of the cantonal parliament from 80 to 60 seats. Shortly after a motion calling to reform the electoral law to better protect smaller parties was submitted. After this the Schaffhausen Government proposed a reform of the electoral system and the implementation of the biproportional apportionment. The biproportional apportionment was also preferred, because of the Supreme Courts decisions in Zurich and Aargau. (Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen , 2007, pp. 1, 3, 13-14) Subsequently the parliament (2007) and the voters (2008) approved the changes. In 2015, the cantonal parliament added a majority clause, which ensures that the strongest party receives at least one seat in the corresponding district. (Lüscher , 2024 , pp. 42- 43) Further did the canton of Schaffhausen decide to prohibit list alliances (Kanton Schaffhausen, 1904/2019, Art. 2b para. 3).

- **2009:** Aargau's voters in the year 2003 approved a proposal in a popular vote, which wanted to lower the amount of parliament seats from 200 to 140. This decision naturally raised the thresholds in the districts and therefore a second constitutional amendment  allowing to merge small districts was proposed and approved by the voters. Though the parliamentarians decided against making use of it. As a consequence of the parliaments decision, the electoral equity wasn't given anymore. The Government of Aargau had to act and proposed to the Grand Council to either merge districts or to change to the Double-Pukelsheim. The Grand Council again decided to not change anything. Shortly after this decision by the Grand Council the FSC issued in a verdict, that there are existing inequalities, because of the varying thresholds and district sizes. The court ordered that this needs to be changed. In September 2007, the Grand Council with a narrow majority then decided to implement the Double-Pukelsheimer. In 2011 a 5% local (district) and a 3% global quorum was added after approval of the Grand Council and the voters (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 38 - 40)

- **2014:** Nidwalden: In the year 2010 members of the Green Party in Nidwalden filed a complaint regarding the seat allocation process for the cantonal elections (Lüscher, 2024, p. 44). That complaint got rejected initially by the Cantonal Court but later the cantonal decision got overruled by the FSC.  The Court rejected the argument that historical practice justified the allocation method. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 44- 45 ;Bundesgericht, 2010a, p.353-364) As a reaction to this decision the parliament of Nidwalden came up with multiple possible reforms. The most popular of the suggested reforms, was the change towards the biproportional system. The parliament and the electorate subsequently approved the implementation of the Double-Pukelsheimer. (Lüscher, 2024, p.45)

- **2014:** Zug: In 2010, representatives of several parties formed a complaint at the FSC regarding the differently sized districts. The Federal Supreme Court agreed on the appeals main point. (Bundesgericht, 2010b, E. 4.5, pp. 378, 385) As a reaction to this decision the cantonal Government presented three different possibilities on how to adapt to the FSC ruling. The responsible comission favoured one option: adopting the Double Pukelsheim. The Parliament adopted the reform and added based on the model of Aargau a 5% local and 3% global threshold. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 47-51 ) A competing proposal to retain the existing system was struck down by the FSC in 2013 (Bundesgericht, 2013, E. 4, pp. 204–205) In addition to the thresholds, the canton also implented a majority clause, ensuring that the most popular list within a district always receives at least one seat (Kanton Zug, 2006/2026, § 52e paras. 1a–1b). Voters approved the biproportional reform on 22 September 2013 (Lüscher, 2024, p. 47-51).

- **2016:** Schwyz: The reform process began with the approval of the new cantonal constitution by the electorate. In that it was foreseen, to keep the current electoral system, which means that each municipality is its own electoral district. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 53) In September 2011, the Cantonal Government prepared the Cantonal Council Election for 2012, against the decisions made there three individual complaints were raised at the FSC. The main complaint was that the thresholds in some of constituencies were too high. The Court agreed on the complaints of the three parties partly and stated that the current electoral system doesn't meet the requirements of a proportional representation system. (Bundesgericht, 2012, Sachverhalt A; E. 5.3 and 6) Later also the Federal Assembly refused to approve the critical sections in the new constitution of Schwyz. As a reaction towards this two different initiatives were formed by the political parties in the canton, one wanted a majority system and the other wanted fairer proportional representation with the willingness to remove guaranteed seats for municipialities. The government reacted with the proposal to inaugurate the DP-System while keeping municipialites as districts and preserving their guaranteed seats. The parliament supported putting the counterproposal together with a 1% global threshold to voters. The voters could then decide on either the majority vote initative or the counterproposal. The counterproposal and with that the implementation of the DP was approved. (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 53-55)

- **2017:** Valais: In the year 2004, a complaint at the FSC was filed regarding the varying thresholds in the electoral districts. The FSC then rejected the complaint and argued that there are historical reasons for the shapes of the electoral districts. (Bundesgericht , 2004, E. 1.1, 2.5 and 3) Six years later an alliance from Upper-Valais proposed the popular initiative "Every Vote Counts" and with that the implementation of the DP with only three new districts. In 2011 the canton then set up a commission to develop proposals. (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 58–59) In 2012 multiple voters again filed a complaint at the Supreme Court it then changed its position and  ruled that the existing system violated the Federal Constitution (Bundesgericht, 2014, Sachverhalt, S. 109 and E. 5.2). The parliament then approved a constitutional reform introducing biproportional seat allocation, but it also added a guarantee of 35 seats for German-speaking Upper Valais. Voters narrowly rejected the package and also the initiative “Every Vote Counts” in 2015. To ensure lawful elections in 2017, parliament unanimously adopted a temporary decree in March 2016 without the seat guarantee. The resulting system retained 14 subdistricts, grouped them into six larger districts, and applied biproportional allocation separately within each larger district. Parliament incorporated these rules into the cantonal electoral law in December 2017. (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 61–63) The Canton Valais also implemented a 8 % local (district-level) threshold (Kanton Wallis, 2004b, Art. 154 Abs. 1).

- **2020:** Uri used a mixed electoral system: municipalities with one or two seats elected their representatives by Majorz, whereas those with at least three seats used proportional representation. A complaint against the seat allocation for the 2016 election led the Federal Supreme Court to rule that the allocation method within the Proporz municipalities violated electoral equality. The Court did not reject the mixed system itself, which it considered justifiable because it preserved personality-oriented elections and an autonomously elected representative for very small municipalities (Bundesgericht, 2016, Sachverhalt, p. 93, E. 5–5.4 and 6.5; Kanton Uri, 2019, pp. 6–7). The government subsequently proposed Double Pukelsheim for all eight municipalities then using proportional representation. During the legislative debate, however, the Landrat raised the threshold for Proporz from three to five seats, moving Attinghausen, Flüelen, Seedorf, and Silenen to Majorz and leaving only Altdorf, Bürglen, Erstfeld, and Schattdorf in the Double Pukelsheim allocation. The parliamentary majority reasoned that Majorz better suited the four municipalities' small populations and strong autonomy. It also pointed to the weak role or absence of local party organizations, occasional uncontested elections, and electoral statistics suggesting that voters chose personalities rather than party lists. The government opposed the extension and, based on a constitutional-law opinion, warned of a high risk that it would fail a renewed challenge before the Federal Supreme Court. Uri's voters approved both the constitutional amendment extending Majorz and the separate Proporzgesetz reform in May 2019 (Kanton Uri, 2019, pp. 4, 10–11; Lüscher, 2024, pp. 64–67).

- **2022:** Graubünden: Before the Implementation of the biproportional apportionment the canton still used a majority based electoral system. Though there were multiple attempts to introduce a PR system. A main reason for these attempts to fail, was the fear that the protection of local minorities and the 20 single-seat-constituencies would be weakened. (Lüscher, 2024, p.69) In 2017 then multiple parties and individuals filed a complaint at the Federal Supreme Court after the cantons government had released the seat allocations for the districts in the upcoming election. The court partially upheld the complaint, it especially decided that the seat allocation for the smallest district (Avers) and the six largest districts needed to be revised. Specifically the Court found that the guaranteed seats for Aver's 160 eligible voters violated equality of voting weight, while majoirtiy voting in the six largest constituencies unjustifiably impaired the equal effect of votes on seat allocation. (Bundesgericht, 2019, Sachverhalt, p. 260, E. 7.3, 8.5, 8.6 and 9) As a response to the FSC decision, the government launched a consultation process after which, it presented nine different models. While the government preferred the DP-System, the municipalities and large parties favoured a mixed electoral model. The willingness of the Socialdemocrats to withdraw a separate initative helped build support for Double-Pukelsheim. The parliament then chose the Double Pukelsheim as a compromise, since it made the seat allocation more proportional while keeping representation for small districts. A 3% global (cantonwide) threshold was also introduced. In addition to the thresholds, the canton added a majority clause similar to the one in Schaffhausen and Zug (Kanton Graubünden, 2021/2026, Art. 28 paras. 2–4). In 2021 the electorate voted in favor of implementing the DP-System. (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 71-72 )

- **2027:** Basel-Landschaft: Unlike other cantons, in Basel-Landschaft there were no implicit quorums of more than 10%, which means that the law complied with the FSC ruling. In 2015 though a parliamentarian requested the cantonal government to examine the comparative effects of the current system with the Double Pukelsheimer. The Government didn't see any need for a reform, the parliamentarian though kept working on the topic and demanded the establishment of a special comission to review the topic. Although the parliament also rejected this proposal, it instructed its executive board to work with external experts to examine how the electoral system could better reflect party vote shares while preserving elected representatives’ local ties. A few years later in 2022, the executive board came to the conclusion, that it recommended the implementation of the DP. Through the support of the parliament, the government was then instructed to draft a revision of the electoral law. (Lüscher, 2024, p.86) In the year 2024, the government then submitted the bill and the Cantonal Council voted in favour of it (Regierungsrat des Kantons Basel-Landschaft, 2024 ; Landrat des Kantons Basel-Landschaft, 2024, p. 1052). The new reform was subject to a mandatory referendum, the canton's voters voted for the implementation in 2025 (Kanton Basel-Landschaft, 2025b). The canton also decided to implement a 3% global and a 5% local threshold and stipulated that each constituency has one guaranteed seat (Kanton Basel-Landschaft, 1981/2025, Art. 39a and Art.49 lit.a). The first election under the new system will be held in 2027 (Kanton Basel-Landschaft, 2026).

To summarize, in 8 of 10 reform cantons, a raised complaint at the FSC led to a later reform. Only the cantons Schaffhausen and Basel-Landschaft reform process took place without a Federal Supreme Court ruling. Nevertheless the canton of Schaffhausen's decision was directly influenced by the FSC's decisions in Aargau and Zurich. Throughout all complaints, the concern was electoral equality. In seven of them excessively high natural thresholds in proportional constituencies were central. While in Graubünden the concerns were mainly raised by the use of of the majority system for its large districts and the allocation of seats among constituencies. This demonstrates the influence of the 2002 Federal Supreme Court decision regarding Zurich's City Parliament.

Beyond their different paths to reform, the cantons also implemented Double Pukelsheim under substantially different institutional conditions. The number of seats included in the Double Pukelsheim allocation varies from 37 in Uri where the system applies only to four municipalities to 180 in Zurich (Standeskanzlei Uri, 2020, p. 1; Kanton Zürich, 2003, § 88).  Moreover, some cantons introduced explicit local or canton-wide electoral quorums, whereas others did not, potentially limiting smaller parties’ ability to benefit from the more proportional allocation method. These arrangements have also changed over time—for example through the later introduction of thresholds or majority clauses—while party competition and vote distributions vary between elections. This institutional variation motivates the exploratory comparisons below: whether smaller parties’ seat-share gains differ by the number of seats allocated through Double Pukelsheim, by the presence of an explicit quorum, and across successive elections within the same canton.

### Literature Review

Building on the institutional mechanisms described above, the existing empirical literature generally finds that Double Pukelsheim improves vote–seat proportionality and benefits parties that were disadvantaged by small electoral districts. However, the studies differ substantially in their research designs, geographical coverage, and treatment of counterfactual electoral rules.

Pukelsheim and Schuhmacher provide an early counterfactual comparison based on the 2011 Zurich election. They apply the former Hagenbach–Bischoff method to the observed votes while assuming four hypothetical list alliances based on political orientations and historical alliances. Under this counterfactual, the larger SVP, SP, and FDP receive additional seats, primarily at the expense of smaller parties such as the BDP and Alternative List. Their calculation also indicates considerably greater inequality in the electoral success of votes under Hagenbach–Bischoff. The analysis nevertheless concerns only one election, and its results depend partly on assumptions about which list alliances parties would have formed. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, pp. 1590–1592)

Lüscher conducts a similar comparison for the 2016 Schwyz election. Under his Hagenbach–Bischoff counterfactual, which does not assume any list alliances, the dominant SVP and CVP would have benefited, whereas the left alliance and especially the GLP benefited from Double Pukelsheim. Most notably, the GLP’s three observed seats would have been reduced to zero under Hagenbach–Bischoff (Lüscher, 2024, p. 13). This example illustrates the potentially substantial effect of the allocation rule on an individual smaller party, but it does not establish whether effects of this magnitude occur systematically across cantons and elections.

Leuzinger broadens the comparison by examining the most recent election in each of the seven cantons that had introduced Double Pukelsheim by 2018. His study is the closest precedent for the present analysis because it calculates hypothetical seat distributions under the former cantonal electoral systems. However, it covers only one election per canton and assumes that the list alliances observed in the final pre-reform election would have persisted (Leuzinger, 2018, p. 42). The present thesis does not carry these historical alliances forward. Consequently, the two counterfactual specifications can produce different Hagenbach–Bischoff seat allocations. This illustrates the sensitivity of counterfactual results to assumptions about unobserved alliance formation. Leuzinger also mentions that he observed, that mainly smaller parties profited from the transition and  that around 10% of the mandates mechanically change the party, through the transition (Leuzinger , 2018, p.42). 

Taken together, the counterfactual calculations by Pukelsheim and Schuhmacher, Lüscher, and Leuzinger constitute the closest methodological precedents for the present thesis. They apply a former allocation rule to votes observed under Double Pukelsheim and compare the resulting counterfactual seat distribution with the actual allocation. Their comparisons therefore hold the observed post-reform vote distribution constant and isolate the difference produced by the allocation rules.

The interpretation of this difference can be clarified using Fiva and Folke’s framework for separating the mechanical and psychological effects of electoral reform. Fiva and Folke examine a reform of Norwegian municipal elections, first applied in 2003, that replaced D’Hondt with modified Sainte-Laguë. (Fiva & Folke, 2016 , p.266) Their principal estimate of the mechanical reform effect compares the actual pre-reform allocation with a counterfactual application of the new formula to the same pre-reform votes. They also apply the former and new formulas to the same post-reform votes to examine how behavioral responses may alter the magnitude of the mechanical effect. (Fiva & Folke, 2016, pp. 270–272) The Swiss studies described above, and the present thesis, follow this latter computational approach: the former formula is applied counterfactually to votes observed under the new system. This measures the mechanical allocation difference conditional on the observed post-reform vote distribution, but it does not estimate how parties and voters would have behaved had the former system remained in place or identify the reform’s complete causal effect. 

Rather than recalculating individual elections, Lüscher’s principal empirical analysis estimates how cantonal political outcomes would have developed without the reforms. He finds that Double Pukelsheim substantially reduced vote–seat disproportionality, with stronger improvements in cantons that previously had smaller average district magnitudes (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 129–143). However, Lüscher finds no significant increase in the effective number of parliamentary parties or electoral candidacies. Voter turnout initially declined slightly, but this effect diminished over subsequent elections. These findings distinguish the reform’s immediate mechanical consequences from its more limited behavioural effects on parties and voters.(Lüscher, 2024, pp. 143–145) 

The existing literature therefore provides strong evidence that Double Pukelsheim improves proportionality, as well as several examples in which smaller parties gain seats. What remains less systematically examined is the magnitude and consistency of the conditional mechanical allocation difference across successive elections. Existing counterfactual studies either focus on individual elections or cover only one election per reform canton, while Lüscher’s longitudinal analysis examines aggregate disproportionality and broader political outcomes rather than the election-specific seat gains of smaller parties.

This thesis addresses that narrower gap by applying a consistent Hagenbach–Bischoff counterfactual to 30 elections in eight transition cantons. Two elections from Graubünden are additionally presented as contextual comparisons. Because Graubünden previously used majority voting rather than Hagenbach–Bischoff, these allocations are hypothetical and are excluded from the main transition estimate. The thesis holds observed post-reform votes constant, applies a common definition of smaller parties, and measures their change in seat share for every election. In contrast to Leuzinger (2018) and Pukelsheim & Schuchmacher (2011), it does not assume that hypothetical or historical pre-reform alliances would have persisted. The analysis therefore estimates the mechanical allocation difference conditional on the observed votes without introducing an additional behavioral assumption about counterfactual alliance formation.


### Expected Effects of the Transition

Based on the theoretical considerations developed in the preceding sections, several effects can be expected from the transition from the Hagenbach–Bischoff method to the Double Pukelsheim system. Under a district-by-district Hagenbach–Bischoff allocation, small district magnitudes create high natural thresholds for winning a parliamentary seat. Votes cast for parties that fail to obtain a seat in a district cannot contribute to their representation elsewhere. This produces ineffective votes, disproportionately disadvantages smaller parties, and may advantage larger parties. Double Pukelsheim instead pools votes across the whole area covered by the upper apportionment before distributing each party's seats among the districts. This should increase the equality of electoral success and reduce vote–seat disproportionality. Mechanically, and conditional on the same observed votes, smaller parties that surpass the applicable legal thresholds are therefore expected to receive a larger seat share under Double Pukelsheim, while the seat advantage previously enjoyed by larger parties should decline (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, pp. 506–508, 513-514 , 518).

The magnitude of this mechanical difference should depend particularly on district magnitude under the Hagenbach–Bischoff comparison. The fewer seats allocated in a district, the larger the vote share a party generally needs to obtain representation. Double Pukelsheim should therefore produce larger gains for smaller parties where the former or counterfactual Hagenbach–Bischoff allocation consists of many low-magnitude districts than where seats are already allocated in relatively large districts. This expectation is consistent with Lüscher's finding that the reduction in disproportionality was stronger in cantons with smaller pre-reform average district magnitudes (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 132–133). 

The effect is also expected to depend on the specific institutional design adopted by each canton. Reflecting Switzerland's federal structure, the reformed cantons differ in their use of canton-wide and district-level legal thresholds ranging from 1 to 8 percent, majority clauses, and other supplementary provisions. Explicit electoral thresholds can restrict gains among smaller parties by excluding lists that do not reach the required vote share and can therefore partly offset the greater proportionality produced by the upper apportionment (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 18; Lüscher, 2024, pp. 107, 135). The expected effect of majority clauses is less unambiguous because they protect the strongest list within a district rather than parties of a particular size; they may modify individual district allocations without systematically benefiting either smaller or larger parties (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 520).

Valais and Uri are particularly important special cases because Double Pukelsheim does not cover the canton through a single canton-wide upper apportionment. Valais conducts separate upper apportionments in six electoral regions, so votes aren't pooled across the entire canton. This is expected to limit the proportionality-enhancing effect relative to a fully canton-wide implementation, particularly for parties whose support is dispersed across regions (Lüscher, 2024, p. 57). In Uri, Double Pukelsheim applies only to Altdorf, Bürglen, Erstfeld, and Schattdorf, while the remaining municipalities use Majorz. This limits the territorial and numerical scope of the reform, although it does not necessarily reduce the mechanical effect among the four municipalities included in the upper apportionment (Kanton Uri, 2019, pp. 4, 10–11; Lüscher, 2024, pp. 64–67).

The total number of seats allocated through Double Pukelsheim may provide further context. All else equal, a larger number of seats allows vote shares to be translated into seat shares more finely (Lüscher, 2024, p. 106). However, parliament size does not generate an unambiguous expectation for the difference between the two allocation methods because the Double Pukelsheim and Hagenbach–Bischoff allocations being compared distribute the same total number of seats. How those seats are divided among districts under Hagenbach–Bischoff is the more direct mechanism. Differences between larger and smaller parliaments should therefore be interpreted as exploratory contextual evidence rather than as an isolated effect of parliament size.

The estimated difference may additionally depend on the electoral rules used to construct the counterfactual outcomes, including the treatment of list alliances and canton-specific allocation provisions. It represents the mechanical allocation difference conditional on the observed post-reform votes, not the reform's complete causal effect on party or voter behaviour. No uniform directional development across successive elections is expected because party vote shares, the parties classified as smaller, district magnitudes, thresholds, and other electoral rules can change over time.

Together, these expectations provide the foundation for the following hypothesis and exploratory questions concerning differences in smaller parties seat shares.


## Hypotheses

To be able to answer the research question: 20 Years of Double Pukelsheim in Switzerland: What Is the Mechanical Effect of the Transition from Hagenbach-Bischoff on the Seat Allocation of Smaller Parties?

To answer the research question, this thesis examines one main hypothesis concerning smaller parties' seat shares. Exploratory comparisons examine differences by district magnitude under the Hagenbach–Bischoff comparison, the number of seats allocated through Double Pukelsheim, the presence of an explicit electoral quorum, and successive elections within each canton. The main hypothesis focuses on the mechanical effect of the electoral reform on smaller parties.


### Hypothesis 1

For each election $e$, smaller parties are those with less than 10% of the vote in the analyzed area: the whole canton except in Uri, where only the four municipalities using Double Pukelsheim are included. Let $S^{DP}_{e}$ and $S^{HB}_{e}$ be their combined seats under Double Pukelsheim and the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation, respectively, and let $M_e$ be the number of seats allocated through Double Pukelsheim and included in the comparison. Their gain in seat share, shown for each election in @fig-small-parties-relative, is

$$
\Delta_e = 100\frac{S^{DP}_{e}-S^{HB}_{e}}{M_e}\quad\text{percentage points}.
$$

The hypothesis uses the unweighted mean, $\bar{\Delta}=E^{-1}\sum_{e=1}^{E}\Delta_e$, so each election counts equally. The analysis also reports a mean weighted by the number of analyzed seats in each election.

**H₁ (main hypothesis):** On average across the analyzed elections, smaller parties receive a larger share of the analyzed seats allocated through Double Pukelsheim than under the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation.

The 10% threshold is based on that the Swiss Federal Supreme Court's reasoning that direct and natural quorums, understood as barriers to representation within an electoral district, should generally not exceed 10% (BGE 131 I 74, E. 5.3–5.5; Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 8).

### Exploratory Questions
#### Exploratory question 1: Differences by district magnitude

Does the gain in smaller parties' seat share under Double Pukelsheim relative to the counterfactual Hagenbach–Bischoff allocation tend to be larger in cantons with smaller electoral districts? District size is measured primarily by the mean district magnitude in the Hagenbach–Bischoff comparison. For election $e$, with $D_e$ districts and district magnitudes $m_{de}$, the mean district magnitude is

$$
\bar{m}_e=\frac{1}{D_e}\sum_{d=1}^{D_e}m_{de}=\frac{M_e}{D_e}.
$$

A lower mean district magnitude is expected to be associated with a larger gain $\Delta_e$ for smaller parties. As a complementary measure, the analysis reports the share of districts with fewer than nine seats,

$$
q_e=\frac{1}{D_e}\sum_{d=1}^{D_e}\mathbb{1}(m_{de}<9).
$$

The nine-seat cutoff follows the Swiss Federal Supreme Court's reasoning: under the natural-quorum approximation $1/(M+1)$, districts with fewer than nine seats impose a threshold above 10%. A larger value of $q_e$ is therefore expected to be associated with a larger gain $\Delta_e$ (BGE 131 I 74, E. 5.3–5.5; Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 8). Because the number of transition cantons is small and their electoral rules differ, these relationships are interpreted descriptively rather than as isolated causal effects of district magnitude. Graubünden is shown only as a contextual comparison because its pre-reform system was Majorz and its Hagenbach–Bischoff allocation is hypothetical (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, Table 1).

#### Exploratory question 2: Differences by DP seat count (Parliament size)

How does the gain in smaller parties' seat share vary between cantons with larger and smaller numbers of seats allocated through Double Pukelsheim? As a contextual comparison, cantons where more than 100 seats are allocated through Double Pukelsheim (ZH, AG, and VS) are compared with cantons where at most 100 seats are allocated through Double Pukelsheim (UR, NW, ZG, SH, and SZ).^[Official seat totals: ZH (Amt für Statistik und Daten Kanton Zürich, 2026); AG (Statistisches Amt Kanton Aargau, n.d.); VS (Kanton Wallis, 2024); UR (Standeskanzlei Uri, 2024b); NW (Staatskanzlei Nidwalden, 2026); ZG (Kanton Zug, 2022c); SH (Staatskanzlei Kanton Schaffhausen, 2024); SZ (Kanton Schwyz, 2024); GR, shown for context (Kanton Graubünden, 2026).] For each canton, the election-level gains $\Delta_e$ are averaged first; the group mean then averages these canton means so that cantons with more observed elections receive no extra weight. Because both allocation methods distribute the same total number of seats and district magnitude is the more direct mechanism, this comparison is interpreted as contextual rather than as an isolated effect of parliament size. Graubünden is shown separately because its pre-reform system was Majorz and its Hagenbach–Bischoff allocation is hypothetical (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, Table 1).

#### Exploratory question 3: Explicit electoral quorums

How does the gain in smaller parties' seat share under Double Pukelsheim relative to the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation vary between elections conducted with and without an explicit electoral quorum?

#### Exploratory question 4: Change across successive elections

How does the gain in smaller parties' seat share under Double Pukelsheim relative to the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation vary across successive elections within each canton? The analysis follows the seat shares under both allocation rules and their difference $\Delta_e$ from each canton's first election under Double Pukelsheim onward. No directional trend is hypothesized, because vote shares, the composition of parties below the 10% threshold, district seat magnitudes, and electoral rules can change between elections.


## Research Design and Analysis {#analysis}

### Research Design and Counterfactual Strategy

Here comes: 

- Actual DP allocation as the observed outcome
- Reconstruction of HB as the counterfactual
- What the comparison identifies: the mechanical effect

H1: The analysis takes the actual seat allocation under the Pukelsheimer Proporz as its starting point. Based on the available election data at the municipal or district level, it then reconstructs how many seats each party would have obtained under the former Hagenbach-Bischoff system. The comparison between the actual seat distribution under the new system and the hypothetical distribution under the old system makes it possible to identify how many seats each party gained or lost as a result of the reform. In this way, the study assesses the mechanical effect of the electoral-system change on party representation, with a particular focus on smaller parties.

### Counterfactual Assumptions and Scope

Here comes:

- former cantonal rules;
- treatment of alliances;
- district structures;
- special cases : GR, ZG, UR, VS, and SH

For the counterfactual, the observed district-level party votes and district seat magnitudes are retained. Where Hagenbach-Bischoff was used before the reform, its allocation is reconstructed under the relevant former cantonal rules, including the former Zurich Wahlgesetz (§§ 87–88b), the pre-reform Aargau legislation, the former Uri Proporzgesetz (Arts. 22–23), and the former Valais law (Arts. 154–156); the canton-specific scripts document the remaining cases (Kanton Zürich, 1983/2005; Kanton Aargau, 2004; Kanton Uri, 2018; Kanton Wallis, 2004a).

The HB allocations in Graubünden and in Zug's Neuheim constituency are hypothetical comparisons rather than reconstructions of their former Majorz rules. The Hagenbach–Bischoff counterfactual allocates seats to the standardized electoral units in each election’s data. Joint lists reported as one unit remain pooled but no additional alliances are assumed between separately reported units. The analysis does not carry alliances from the last pre-reform election forward, unlike Leuzinger (2018, p. 42).

As already initially explained in the Introduction, this study does not follow Leuzinger’s or the approach of Pukelsheim and Schuhmacher of carrying historical or hypothetical list alliances forward into the counterfactual allocation. List alliances are in this thesis seen as strategic and election-specific rather than fixed institutional parameters. Their formation depends on the parties contesting an election, their relative electoral strength, ideological proximity, district-level incentives, and expectations about possible seat gains (SOURCE?). In Zurich, for example, the last Kantonsrat election under Hagenbach–Bischoff took place in 2003. Assuming that the alliances formed in 2003 would still have applied in 2023 despite two decades of changes in the party system would therefore introduce a strong and unverifiable behavioural assumption. Some parties that formed list alliances in Zurich in 2003 no longer existed or contested the 2023 election. Conversely, parties such as the Green Liberal Party, which contested the 2023 election, did not yet exist in 2003. (Statistisches Amt des Kantons Zürich 2003, table 3; Statistisches Amt des Kantons Zürich 2026; Grünliberale Partei Kanton Zürich n.d.). Therefore the counterfactual preserves joint lists or list groups represented as a single unit in the observed election data. But it does not reconstruct historical alliances or assume new alliances between separately reported units. This provides a transparent counterfactual that holds the observed electoral configuration constant and isolates the mechanical consequences of applying Hagenbach–Bischoff.

The decision not to carry historical list alliances forward or to create hypothetical ones does not imply that parties would have contested the election without alliances under Hagenbach–Bischoff. Rather, their counterfactual alliance decisions cannot be reliably observed or reconstructed. Because alliances can mitigate the disadvantages experienced by smaller parties under Hagenbach–Bischoff (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1590), excluding unobserved alliances may affect the estimated magnitude of the resulting seat changes.

::: {.callout-note title="Scope of the canton comparisons"}
**Graubünden.** The canton used Majorz throughout before adopting Double Pukelsheim. Its HB allocation is hypothetical, so the observations are shown in grey and excluded from the main transition estimate (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, Table 1, p. 14).

**Zug.** Neuheim used Majorz before the reform, while the other ten municipalities used proportional allocation. Neuheim participates in the observed canton-wide Double Pukelsheim allocation, so all 80 seats are retained. The HB allocation for Neuheim is a hypothetical uniform-HB comparison, not a reconstruction of its former Majorz rule (Bundesgericht, 2010b, E. 5.1; Kanton Zug, 2022a, 2022b, 2022c).

**Uri.** Only Altdorf, Bürglen, Erstfeld, and Schattdorf used Double Pukelsheim in the elections analyzed here. They account for 37 of the Landrat's 64 seats; the remaining municipalities used Majorz and are excluded from both allocations in this comparison (Standeskanzlei Uri, 2020, p. 1). Uri's vote shares, including the less-than-10% classification of smaller parties, are therefore based only on the four municipalities using Double Pukelsheim, not on the whole canton.

**Valais.** Upper apportionment takes place separately within six electoral regions. If for example, the SVP/UDC contested all six regions, it would enter six independent regional allocations; votes in one region cannot increase its seat entitlement in another. This analysis sums the resulting regional seats under one canton-wide party label and aggregates voter numbers to calculate canton-wide vote shares. The single party row and the classification of parties below 10% are therefore measures for comparison, not the regional units used to allocate seats (Lüscher, 2024, p. 57).

**Schaffhausen** reduced its parliament from 80 to 60 seats for the first Double Pukelsheim election. The counterfactual holds the later election's 60-seat district structure fixed, so it isolates the allocation method under that structure rather than reproducing every feature of the 2004 election (Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 2007, pp. 1, 6).
:::

- Refer detailed canton-specific cleaning procedures and code to the Appendix.

To be able to analyze the data from the different elections and compare the outcomes. each dataset has to be cleaned. The data  For some cantons e.g. Valais and Schwyz the data is very scattered, therefore for there multiple datasets per election have to be cleaned and merged.

The procedure for the data cleaning was the following: For each canton in alphabetical order, for each election the data was cleaned.

To ensure the compatibility of the different datasets, the column names were standardized. The column names were renamed for each dataset to the following: "total_votes", "svp_votes", "sp_votes", "cvp_votes", "fdp_votes", "glp_votes", "bdp_votes", "green_votes", "other_votes". It might be that some of the datasets do not contain all of these columns, since the party landscapes varies geographically and over time. 

Vote shares for the analyzed area are derived from the available official *Wählerzahl* or reported vote-share figures; where necessary, the cleaning scripts reconstruct voter numbers from district-level party votes and seat magnitudes.

The calculation and rounding procedures vary by canton and source file.

The official Double Pukelsheim results (`seats_dp`) are sourced from official cantonal authorities and are documented in the Bibliography. A single lookup table consolidates all official results for easy merging with the Hagenbach-Bischoff counterfactuals. All data processing is implemented in canton-specific R scripts (R/canton_*.R) which apply shared functions for algorithm execution and validation.
```{r data-setup}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Load packages for data processing, plotting, labels, and source files.
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)
library(here)

# Load the allocation functions and canton-specific cleaning scripts.
# Suppress validation tables printed while sourcing them.
invisible(capture.output({
  source(here("data_cleaning_cantons", "00_functions.R"))
  source(here("data_cleaning_cantons", "canton_AG.R"))
  source(here("data_cleaning_cantons", "canton_GR.r"))
  source(here("data_cleaning_cantons", "canton_NW.R"))
  source(here("data_cleaning_cantons", "canton_SZ.R"))
  source(here("data_cleaning_cantons", "canton_VS.R"))
  source(here("data_cleaning_cantons", "canton_ZG.R"))
  source(here("data_cleaning_cantons", "canton_ZH.R"))
  source(here("data_cleaning_cantons", "canton_UR.R"))
  source(here("data_cleaning_cantons", "canton_SH.R"))
}))

# Run each canton's cleaning and seat-allocation pipeline.
ag_clean <- process_canton_AG()
gr_clean <- process_canton_GR()
nw_clean <- process_canton_NW()
sz_clean <- process_canton_SZ()
vs_clean <- process_canton_VS()
zg_clean <- process_canton_ZG()
zh_clean <- process_canton_ZH()
ur_clean <- process_canton_UR()
sh_clean <- process_canton_SH()
# Use one party-by-election dataset for the figures below.
all_elections <- bind_rows(
  ag_clean,
  gr_clean,
  nw_clean,
  sz_clean,
  vs_clean,
  zg_clean,
  zh_clean,
  ur_clean,
  sh_clean
)


```

### Measures and Analytical Strategy 

Here comes:

- Smaller party definition and 10% cutoff.
- Unit of analysis: election, and analyzed area
- Definition and interpretation of \(\Delta_e\).
- Unweighted mean used for H1.
- Seat-weighted mean as supplementary information.
- Distributional statistics reported.
- Procedure for the DP-seat-count comparison.
- Procedure for the quorum comparison.
- Procedure for examining successive elections.
- Graubünden’s exclusion from the main estimate.
- why seats_allocated_dp is the denominator

For the purposes of this thesis, a smaller party is defined as an electoral list or list group with a vote share below 10% in the analyzed area. The analyzed area is equal to the whole canton except in Uri, where the vote shares cover only the four municipalities using Double Pukelsheim. Youth lists and other special-interest lists, such as women’s lists or pensioners’ lists, are treated as separate analytical units whenever they are reported separately in the official election results; their votes and seats are not attributed to a parent party. Accordingly, the term *party* in the analysis refers to the standardized electoral list or list group recorded in the dataset and does not necessarily correspond to a broader organizational party family.
The choice of 10% as the threshold is grounded in both legal and normative considerations. In its decision BGE 131 I 74, the Swiss Federal Supreme Court argued that direct and natural quorums, understood as barriers to representation within an electoral district, should generally not exceed 10% (E. 5.3–5.5; see also Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 8). Using vote share rather than absolute party size is particularly appropriate because a party may be electorally small in one region while being comparatively strong in another. Low thresholds are closely linked to the principle of Erfolgswertgleichheit which is the equality in the effect of votes on seat allocation, which requires that votes should be translated into seats as equally and effectively as possible (BGE 131 I 74, E. 3.1; Bundeskanzlei, 2013, pp. 8–9).
This threshold is especially relevant to the cantons analyzed here: before their reforms, each had at least one district with an electoral threshold of 10% or higher (Lüscher, 2024, p. 115).


### Results

#### Main result: Smaller Parties seat-share gain

@fig-small-parties-absolute compares the observed Double Pukelsheim allocation with the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation for every cleaned election. For each election, the figure aggregates the seats and vote shares in the analyzed area of all parties below the 10% threshold defined above. The grey line connects the two allocations derived from the same election.

```{r}
#| label: fig-small-parties-absolute
#| fig-cap: "Seats won by smaller parties under Double Pukelsheim and the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation. Smaller parties have less than 10% of the vote share in the analyzed area."
#| fig-width: 8.3
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Restrict the tie check to parties below the 10% vote-share threshold.
small_party_rows <- all_elections |>
  filter(small_party == 1L)

# A slash marks alternative HB seat totals from an unresolved draw.
if (any(str_detect(small_party_rows$seats_hb, fixed("/")))) {
  stop("Resolve smaller-party HB ties before plotting.")
}

# Aggregate smaller parties within each election under both seat rules.
small_party_summary <- all_elections |>
  group_by(election_id) |>
  summarise(
    parliament_size = first(parliament_size),
    seats_allocated_dp = first(seats_allocated_dp),
    vote_share_small_parties = sum(vote_share[small_party == 1L]),
    # Only smaller-party seats enter the HB–DP comparison.
    seats_hb = sum(as.integer(seats_hb[small_party == 1L])),
    seats_dp = sum(seats_dp[small_party == 1L]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    is_graubuenden = str_starts(election_id, "GR_"),
    # Express the DP gain as a share of seats included in the comparison.
    seat_gain_pp = 100 * (seats_dp - seats_hb) / seats_allocated_dp,
    gain_label = sprintf("%s (%+.1f pp)", election_id, seat_gain_pp)
  )

# Put both systems on separate rows for plotting and calculate seat shares.
small_party_plot_data <- small_party_summary |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(seats_hb, seats_dp),
    names_to = "system",
    values_to = "seats_small_parties"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    seat_share_small_parties = 100 * seats_small_parties / seats_allocated_dp,
    # Fix the legend order across both figures.
    system = factor(recode(system, seats_hb = "Hagenbach-Bischoff", seats_dp = "Double Pukelsheim"),
                    levels = c("Hagenbach-Bischoff", "Double Pukelsheim"))
  )

# Summarize election-level gains and the mean weighted by analyzed seats.
h1_stats <- small_party_summary |>
  filter(!is_graubuenden) |>
  summarise(
    elections = n(), mean_gain = mean(seat_gain_pp),
    weighted_mean_gain = weighted.mean(seat_gain_pp, seats_allocated_dp),
    q1 = quantile(seat_gain_pp, .25), median = median(seat_gain_pp),
    q3 = quantile(seat_gain_pp, .75),
    above_five = sum(seat_gain_pp > 5)
  )

# Draw either the seat-count or seat-share version of the same comparison.
small_party_plot <- function(x, x_title, label, percent = FALSE) {
  # Label both systems for counts, but only DP points for the denser share plot.
  label_data <- if (percent) filter(small_party_plot_data, system == "Double Pukelsheim") else small_party_plot_data
  ggplot(small_party_plot_data, aes(x = .data[[x]], y = vote_share_small_parties,
                                   color = system, shape = system)) +
    # Connect the two outcomes from each election.
    geom_line(aes(group = election_id), color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_point(data = filter(small_party_plot_data, !is_graubuenden), size = 3.2) +
    geom_point(data = filter(small_party_plot_data, is_graubuenden),
           color = "grey60", shape = 16, size = 3.2) +
    # Place election or gain labels without overlapping points.
    geom_text_repel(data = filter(label_data, !is_graubuenden),
            aes(label = .data[[label]]), size = 3.2,
                    show.legend = FALSE, max.overlaps = Inf, box.padding = 0.3,
                    point.padding = 0.2, segment.color = "grey80",
                    segment.linewidth = 0.4, seed = 2026) +
    geom_text_repel(data = filter(label_data, is_graubuenden),
            aes(label = .data[[label]]), color = "grey60", size = 3.2,
            show.legend = FALSE, max.overlaps = Inf, box.padding = 0.3,
            point.padding = 0.2, segment.color = "grey80",
            segment.linewidth = 0.4, seed = 2026) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("Hagenbach-Bischoff" = "#D55E00",
                                  "Double Pukelsheim" = "#0072B2")) +
    # Format the x-axis as percentages only in the relative figure.
    scale_x_continuous(labels = if (percent) \(x) paste0(x, "%") else waiver(),
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.08))) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.10))) +
    labs(title = "Representation of Smaller Parties Across Elections",
         subtitle = "Observed Double Pukelsheim and counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocations",
         x = x_title, y = "Aggregated vote share of smaller parties (%)",
         color = "Electoral system", shape = "Electoral system") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_text(size = 11),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11), axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

# Plot absolute smaller-party seat totals.
small_party_plot("seats_small_parties", "Number of seats won by smaller parties", "election_id")
```

#### Election-level variation

@fig-small-parties-relative shows the same elections using the percentage of analyzed Double Pukelsheim seats won by smaller parties on the x-axis. Each label reports the gain under Double Pukelsheim as a change in seat share, expressed in percentage points.

```{r}
#| label: fig-small-parties-relative
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of analyzed seats won by smaller parties under Double Pukelsheim and counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff."
#| fig-width: 8.3
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Reuse the plot with seat shares and percentage-point gain labels.
small_party_plot("seat_share_small_parties", "Seats won by smaller parties (%)", "gain_label", TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Hypothesis 1 summary"}
Across all `r h1_stats$elections` elections (Graubünden excluded), the unweighted mean gain in smaller parties' share of analyzed seats was `r sprintf("%.1f", h1_stats$mean_gain)` percentage points (Q1: `r sprintf("%.1f", h1_stats$q1)`; median: `r sprintf("%.1f", h1_stats$median)`; Q3: `r sprintf("%.1f", h1_stats$q3)`). The mean weighted by each election's number of analyzed seats was `r sprintf("%.1f", h1_stats$weighted_mean_gain)` percentage points. `r h1_stats$above_five` individual elections exceeded five percentage points.
:::

#### Exploratory comparison 1: Double Pukelsheim seat count

The comparison below uses the same election-level percentage-point gain as H1. It averages elections within each canton before comparing the two groups defined by the number of seats allocated through Double Pukelsheim. Graubünden is only shown for context and excluded from the group means for the same reason as in the main H1 estimate.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-h1a-cantons
#| tbl-cap: "Mean gain in smaller parties' share of analyzed seats by canton (percentage points). Source: author's aggregation of the official cantonal election datasets."
#| echo: false

h1a_cantons <- small_party_summary |>
  mutate(canton = str_sub(election_id, 1L, 2L)) |> 
  group_by(canton) |>
  summarise(
    elections = n(),
    dp_seats = first(seats_allocated_dp),
    parliament_seats = first(parliament_size),
    mean_gain_pp = mean(seat_gain_pp),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
 mutate(
  size_group = case_when(
    canton == "GR" ~ "Context only (former Majorz)",
    dp_seats > 100L ~ "More than 100 DP seats",
    TRUE ~ "At most 100 DP seats"
  )
) |>
arrange(desc(dp_seats), canton)

h1a_groups <- h1a_cantons |>
  filter(canton != "GR") |>
  group_by(size_group) |>
  summarise(cantons = n(), mean_gain_pp = mean(mean_gain_pp), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable( 
  h1a_cantons |>
    transmute(Canton = canton, Group = size_group,
              Elections = elections,
              `DP seats (parliament)` = paste0(dp_seats, " (", parliament_seats, ")"),
              `Mean gain (pp)` = sprintf("%.1f", mean_gain_pp))
)
```

The mean of the canton-level gains is `r sprintf("%.1f", h1a_groups$mean_gain_pp[h1a_groups$size_group == "More than 100 DP seats"])` percentage points in the group with more than 100 Double Pukelsheim seats and `r sprintf("%.1f", h1a_groups$mean_gain_pp[h1a_groups$size_group == "At most 100 DP seats"])` percentage points in the group with at most 100. Their difference (more than 100 minus at most 100) is `r sprintf("%+.1f", h1a_groups$mean_gain_pp[h1a_groups$size_group == "More than 100 DP seats"] - h1a_groups$mean_gain_pp[h1a_groups$size_group == "At most 100 DP seats"])` percentage points. With only `r sum(h1a_groups$cantons)` cantons and distinct electoral rules, this is a descriptive comparison rather than evidence of a causal effect of the number of Double Pukelsheim seats.

## Appendix

### Appendix 1: Explanation Data Cleaning Process

The table below lists the official election-result sources used in the canton-specific cleaning scripts. It includes raw data inputs and official publications used to reconstruct or validate reported results; legal and methodological sources used only to specify the counterfactual allocation rules are excluded.

```{=typst}
#figure(
  kind: table,

    table.header(
      [*Canton*],

    ),

    [Statistisches Amt Kanton Aargau, *Grossratswahlen: Detailresultate, ab 1985* (elections 2009, 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024); Department für Finanzen und Ressourcen des Kantons Aargau (2009) and Regierungsrat des Kantons Aargau (2013) for validation of the 2009 and 2012 cantonal seat totals; Staatskanzlei des Kantons Aargau (2012, 2016) for the district seat magnitudes.],
    [Graubünden],
    [Kanton Graubünden, *Pressedaten Proporzwahl kantonal: Grossratswahlen* (official Excel workbooks for 2022 and 2026).],

    [Valais],
    [Staat Wallis, official district-level Grand Council result workbooks (2017, 2021, and 2025); official final results for 2017; Grand Council validation-commission reports for the constitutive sessions of April 2021 and April 2025; Kanton Wallis publications on district seat magnitudes for 2017, 2021, and 2025.],
    [Zug],
```
